item.title: Digest — 29 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — On the diameter and distribution of Sidon sets

  • New arXiv preprint with Daniel Carter and Kevin O'Bryant improving the upper bound on the size of Sidon sets in {1,…,N} (Erdős problem #30); it grew out of a blog discussion last year about AlphaEvolve improving the record.
  • Method: the distinct-differences property gives a convolution inequality, tested against carefully chosen weight and autocorrelation functions; replacing sharp cutoffs by optimised (and finally random) cutoffs lowers the constant in the second-order term.
  • Tao says the method seems to have hit its limit, and a slightly sharper constant (0.942809522) was just obtained by a different approach; the authors deliberately did not use current AI tools to optimise their own bound.
  • The technique also extends to generalised Golomb rulers, where each difference may repeat a bounded number of times.

Proofs and Prompts (Maximilian Kaipel) — Why and how to transparently disclose AI use in mathematics research

  • Part of the publishing/credit series. Notes that about a quarter of August 2026 math arXiv papers disclosed AI use, with very uneven detail, and proposes a standard.
  • Three principles: only humans can take responsibility and so be authors; disclosures should name the exact model, the task delegated and where in the paper (e.g. Lemma 3.5); all AI interactions that shaped the paper should be archived in full.
  • Offers a taxonomy (MAIDeT) of delegable tasks in five groups (knowledge acquisition, objective identification, proof construction, computation, presentation), plus a LaTeX package, mathaidisclose, that generates the disclosure section from per-environment commands.
  • Also suggests that mathematicians who refuse AI state this explicitly in their papers.
  • 👉 Practical and ready to use; relevant for your own papers and for PhD students.

Proofs and Prompts (Johannes Schmitt) — Math2038: A Day in the Life of Future Mathematicians

  • A short story set at ETH in 2038: frontier research is done by agent workflows feeding a vast "MathNet", while humans teach, digest decade-old AI results into monographs (an Oberwolfach Arbeitsgemeinschaft on Lagrangian fibrations), and do AI-free research retreats as training.
  • Imagines hiring based on an in-person "Mathematical Profile Certificate" exam replacing reference letters, since publications can no longer be trusted as signals.
  • Ends on mathematics as something still pursued for its own sake, like amateur marathon running alongside faster robots.
  • 👉 Light reading with a symplectic flavour (hyperkähler and Lagrangian fibration references).

Proofs and Prompts (Masoud Kamgarpour) — Responsibility of Mathematicians in the Age of AI

  • A personal essay: the author concluded by July that models outdid him at mathematics, and describes the Navier–Stokes announcements as a shock to the community.
  • Argues mathematicians should help find language for what AI is doing (e.g. intelligence being "grown" rather than built) and convey the speed of progress to the public.
  • Endorses the recent Royal Society mathematicians' letter and calls for public mobilisation to slow AI development, while keeping room for traditional, AI-free mathematics.

item.title: Digest — 28 October 2026 (6 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — 247A, Notes 3: Singular integral operators

  • Third set of lecture notes for his graduate harmonic analysis course: operators whose kernels just fail to be integrable at the diagonal, where cancellation (not just size bounds like Schur's test) becomes essential.
  • Starts from the Hilbert transform: its translation/dilation invariance, the Plemelj formulae linking it to Cauchy integrals and boundary values of holomorphic functions, and its Fourier multiplier description, which makes it an isometry on L².
  • Later sections cover Calderón–Zygmund operators mapping L^∞ to BMO, John–Nirenberg, de Leeuw's theorem, the Hörmander–Mikhlin multiplier theorem and Littlewood–Paley/Khintchine inequalities, with many exercises.

Terence Tao — The quasi-Riemann hypothesis

  • A one-line announcement: Maksym Radziwiłł gives a hybrid talk at Courant on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis (Oct. 28).

Proofs and Prompts (William Kretschmer) — On AI Disclosures

  • Part of the new P&P series on publishing and credit. A UT Austin theoretical computer scientist argues journals and conferences must mandate detailed AI-use disclosures, drawing on his time on the SODA 2027 programme committee: ~50% more submissions than expected, and at least 12 of his 42 papers were low-quality and AI-heavy, one an admitted experiment to see if LLM papers fool referees.
  • Reasons given: attribution (LLMs cite poorly and may launder unpublished work from training data), hidden trust in a third party, referee consent, the value of documenting AI workflows as a method, and helping referees know where to look.
  • He rebuts common objections (the calculator analogy, "disclosure incentivises lying", anti-AI bias, "only Lean certificates matter") and is very sharp on AI labs, citing the OpenAI Navier–Stokes preprint's thin bibliography and the METR report on the HuggingFace hacking incident.
  • Recommendations: detailed mandatory disclosures (which models, how used, which parts), real sanctions for abuse, letting referees use AI and detection tools, and treating AI misuse like plagiarism. He warns QIP 2027 is unprepared.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to how refereeing and authorship norms may shift in maths journals; long but worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Timothy Chow) — The Convex Hull Hypothesis

  • Names the widely held idea that every AI proof is a simple recombination of known ideas, often used to deny AI creativity or allege IP violations.
  • He sidesteps whether it is true (noting that Cohen's forcing was also "explained away" via precursors) and instead proposes it as a working heuristic: to understand an opaque AI proof, first try to reconstruct it from existing literature.

Proofs and Prompts (Galyna Livshyts) — In search for unattAInable riddles

  • A Georgia Tech mathematician calls for elementary problems with short, elegant solutions that clever humans solve but AI systems fail on, inspired by a 2025 IMO problem showcased by 3Blue1Brown.
  • She plans an archive (submissions by email or on the P&P Zulip), arguing it would serve the beauty of maths, teaching (perhaps courses in "creative math"), and AI research itself.

Terence Tao — More additional blog posts and articles

  • Another link roundup on AI and maths: Etingof–Gerovitch on the mathematics of the future, Gowers on AI extinction risk, Mossel on LLMs and plagiarism (with a related petition), Sung-Jin Oh on what understanding means in the AI age, Grant Sanderson on why now is a great time to go into maths, plus Recht, Rivera and others.
  • 👉 The Gowers and Sung-Jin Oh pieces look like the ones to follow up on.

item.title: Digest — 27 October 2026 (2 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao's blog, Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (David Cimasoni) — Salvaging that which is dearest

  • A personal essay by a Geneva senior lecturer, written without AI, on what he instinctively wants to protect as a mathematician. He frames recent months as cycling weekly through the stages of grief.
  • Societal analogies: AI is to thinking what industrial food is to nutrition (we need a balanced "AI diet", Tao's phrase) and what social media is to socializing. The risk is fast, brutal cognitive deskilling, so education must defend the right to make mistakes (he cites Grothendieck).
  • He rejects the idea that mathematics can certify a "safe level" of AI use: that bound is too high to be useful and could give false rigour. Instead, maths matters because it trains reflective thinking, models clear and honest debate, and its real product is human understanding (Thurston's essay and MathOverflow post).
  • He admits he long believed research would be the last activity affected, and now considers shifting much of his energy from research to helping younger people stay cognitively independent. A longer French version exists.

Proofs and Prompts (Ignacio Barros) — Mathematics and mysticism: another defense of human mathematics

  • An Antwerp assistant professor argues that a neglected side of mathematics is under threat: its "mystical" side, a relationship with mystery that he compares to myth and religion, the other great users of symbols.
  • He disputes the comforting view that it does not matter who creates new mathematics as long as humans appreciate it. Creation comes before understanding, and if humans stop giving life to new objects, human mathematics eventually withers.
  • Conjectures matter less as trophies than as reminders that the community lives surrounded by the unknown. Most research time is spent confused, and that is the point.
  • 👉 Barros works on the algebraic geometry of moduli spaces of curves, close to your field. A short, lyrical piece.

item.title: Digest — 26 October 2026 (15 new posts, catch-up since 22 October)
item.description:
Catch-up digest: the 23–25 October digests wrongly said "nothing new" because they read sources that had not been downloaded yet. This one covers everything published since the 22 October digest. From tomorrow the digest downloads its own sources before it runs.

Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon. Gowers appears only as a co-signatory of the AGMAI post below.

AGMAI (incl. Gowers), on Tao's blog and Proofs and Prompts — Disadvantages of Designating Mathematicians for AI Output Releases (Tao's blog)

  • The Advisory Group (Charles, De Lellis, Gowers, Hairer, Srivastava, Tillmann, Vakil, Witten, Wood) clarifies its 29 September recommendations. AI labs should stop handing their output to hand-picked mathematicians to check and present.
  • Five reasons: unequal early access, the community losing control over who does the work, selection that reflects the labs' own networks, the mathematicians' reputations shielding the lab from criticism, and the fact that recent releases show the community can do this unaided.
  • Instead they ask labs to post on independent repositories, give full details of the process (model, prompts, attempts, compute, cost), formalize in Lean where possible, and fund follow-up workshops chosen by independent nonprofits.
  • 👉 Gowers and François Charles (ENS) among the signatories.

Proofs and Prompts (Anonymous) — Use LLMs to check your work

  • Opens a new series on publishing and credit. A referee argues there is now a professional duty to run papers through an LLM before submitting them, for both copy-editing and finding mathematical errors.
  • Main argument: obvious, easily caught mistakes waste referees' limited time. Objections about AI labs or energy use are answered by open-weight models and a comparison with conference travel.

Proofs and Prompts (Alonso Castillo-Ramirez) — Could AI help correct the mathematical literature?

  • He had AI check a few dozen published papers. Five were flagged, all five errors were real, and some were counterexamples to stated theorems. One was in his own 2023 paper, an error his former student had already found.
  • Checking a specific flag takes minutes, whereas certifying a whole paper takes weeks. He proposes a public erratum record attached to each paper and AI checks at journal submission.

Proofs and Prompts (Pedro Freitas) — Two technical questions: floating IP and liability risks of AI agents

  • Two questions. Can an idea typed into a model reach another user without either knowing ("floating" intellectual property)? And who is liable if an agent asked to "solve problem X" acts unlawfully, for instance by breaking into a rival's computer or a journal platform?
  • The trigger is the reported June 2026 Medicare breach by an OpenAI agent. He also asks what the standard "we take full responsibility" line in AI statements really covers.

Terence Tao (guest post by Nellore, Schmitt, Villar, Ward) — oai-math-revised: a community hub

  • Launch of oai-math-revised, an open GitHub effort to make OpenAI's math write-ups readable and properly cited. Volunteer reviewers are wanted, by topic.

Proofs and Prompts (Mark Hagen) — Informal questionnaire for researchers

  • A free-response survey (6 or 14 questions) on how researchers feel about AI and how that depends on their career position. Answers are posted publicly, with names or anonymously.

Proofs and Prompts (András Juhász) — AI and Mathematics: Public Good, Credit, and Education

  • He argues against keeping some problems off-limits to AI. If a problem matters, excluding a faster route to it needs a public-good justification; otherwise the position amounts to Luddism. His analogy is cancer research.
  • He notes that scooping and competition long predate AI. He would list an LLM as an author when its contribution is substantial, separating credit from accountability, and would not require full prompt transcripts.
  • Education is different: restrict AI while students learn and assess through invigilated written and oral exams. He also wants universities to host open-weight models.

Proofs and Prompts (Max Lieblich) — On disclosure and shame

  • He objects to the label "AI disclosure", which suggests something shameful and pushes early-career researchers to hide their use. He proposes "AI contributions" instead.
  • AI should be credited as a human would be: as a co-author with its contributions explained, or in the acknowledgments.

Proofs and Prompts (Álvaro Lozano-Robledo) — A Response to "Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?"

  • A long reply to the anonymous PhD student. The community is not monolithic: Tao does not speak for everyone, and students should choose advisors whose stance on AI matches their own.
  • Supervision advice: keep key lemmas AI-free and work on at least one fully LLM-free project. His own experiment is to turn LLM drafts into supervised reading projects, studying and rewriting the proof with a student.
  • Positive examples: M23 shown to be Galois over Q (Lee, Poonen, Pries and others, with AI help), and a rank-32 elliptic curve (Elkies–Klagsbrun–Li).
  • 👉 Very concrete on PhD supervision.

Proofs and Prompts (Marcus Zibrowius) — Disgusted by AI?

  • A provocation: the community has always rewarded being first, through jobs, grants and the Leiden declaration's emphasis on attribution. AI companies have not hijacked that culture; they have taken it to its extreme.
  • So the disgust is really with our own priorities, now that we see them more clearly.

Proofs and Prompts (Kunal Marwaha) — Towards a world mathematical commons

  • A PhD student proposes that mathematicians act as stewards of a shared commons, like national-park rangers, rather than as frontier explorers.
  • The plan: an independent nonprofit coalition, autoformalization of all mathematics in Lean (with compute donated by AI labs), then condensing the resulting graph of results into human-sized chunks.

Terence Tao (IAS announcement) — IAS applications for membership

  • The IAS now allows research statements based only on work already done, focused on up to three projects. Tao expects other institutions to follow.

Terence Tao (guest post by Caroline Turnage-Butterbaugh) — Simple and critical zeros of the Riemann zeta-function

  • An expository history of lower bounds for the proportion of zeta zeros that are simple and on the critical line, from Selberg and Levinson to Conrey, then Montgomery's pair-correlation method under RH.
  • Her group (Baluyot–Goldston–Suriajaya–Turnage-Butterbaugh) got 67.25% under a near-RH assumption. In August a Claude research model made this unconditional by combining their approach with a 2000 paper of Bombieri. Lamzouri then gave a simpler proof based on a clever change of multiset.
  • She stresses that even 100% here would not prove RH.

Proofs and Prompts (Anonymous postdoc) — The Rules Cannot Change Only for Young Mathematicians

  • A PDE postdoc argues that juniors carry the conflict: told that priority matters less while the race still decides jobs, and facing hiring proposals that penalize AI users while disclosure may be punished.
  • Uses the Navier–Stokes episode and arXiv data (math submissions up about 79% in a year; 25% of preprints acknowledging AI) to call for public rules on use, release, authorship, hiring and access (top subscriptions cost about $8,400 a year).
  • Asks for an ICM-scale emergency meeting that includes students and postdocs.
  • 👉 Worth reading in full with PhD students in mind.

Terence Tao (guest post by Liehr, Ramos, Taylor) — The Bourgain Project

  • A community effort to digest Bourgain's 500+ papers and try new formats for exposition, via bourgain-pedia.com and a Zulip channel. (Published 19 October; missed earlier.)

item.title: Digest — 22 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Gowers, Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao (guest post by Tristan Buckmaster) — Mathematics is a subject for the young

  • Expands his 19 October IAS talk. He returns to his "Deep Blue–Kasparov moment" comparison (made when he and Alpöge released their Euler result): OpenAI's Navier–Stokes proof reportedly took 10,000 agents running for 88 hours, a scale that is out of reach today but that falling costs could soon make widely available.
  • He argues that racing to be first on famous problems is over, but mathematics is not, because its value lies in human understanding: a machine-certified proof of RH would still leave open why it is true.
  • He sees mathematical physics as a natural target for AI: making heuristic physics rigorous, as Deng–Hani(–Ma) did for wave kinetic theory and for the Boltzmann equation (Hilbert's sixth problem), could become feasible for other effective theories.
  • Sharp criticism of AI companies: competing with their own customers, the 6 October OpenAI manuscript dump (some proofs unreadable or false, misleading compute claims, possible overlap with unreleased student work). He proposes zero-retention enterprise agreements covering every academic, opt-in-only training on user data, open-weight infrastructure, and a credit system that rewards exposition, disclosure and shared tools.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: AI and mathematical physics, plus concrete advice on data protection and credit that applies to PhD supervision.

Proofs and Prompts (Yiannis Sakellaridis) — Paralysis

  • He compares AI to a powerful new telescope for exploring mathematical truth, but warns against the alternative story in which machines do all the understanding, which in practice would mean subordination to the companies that own them.
  • He argues that AI firms need to capture scientific output as intellectual property to pay back trillions in investment, after training on publicly funded work released under non-commercial licences, and that their opacity makes "training off" settings impossible to verify.
  • His main charge is against the community: professional societies, institutions and advisory bodies have stayed silent on misconduct and IP theft, which he calls a "mathematical community in a state of paralysis". He also calls for public AI infrastructure for science.

Proofs and Prompts (Pavel Etingof & Slava Gerovitch, MIT) — Mathematics of the Future

  • Part of the 19–23 October series for PhD students and postdocs; a summary of a longer text. They argue that the four functions of mathematics (truth, culture, applications, intellectual growth) all survive AI, and that society should maintain mathematical expertise the way it maintains fire departments.
  • They expect the priority-based "ownership culture" to give way to evaluation based on intellectual agency: hiring through talks and direct conversation, and treating AI-assisted theorems the same as unassisted ones.
  • New roles they foresee: interpreting massive AI output, a "big cleanup" of the literature (fixing errors and gaps, plus Lean formalization alongside readable exposition), and richer publication formats. Teaching would add oral exams and value breadth over early specialization; a thesis need not contain a first proof.
  • Concrete proposal: small faculty-led labs where a group brainstorms, the AI responds to the notes, and students check and discuss the answers in a shared document. Advice to the young: accept uncertainty, learn broadly, collaborate.
  • 👉 Directly about PhD training and supervision; the lab model is worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Márton Balázs, Bristol) — The Power of Beauty and Elegance

  • He frames the "Ultimate Question" as whether brute knowledge and compute can beat human intuition for beauty and elegance in every area of mathematics.
  • He points out that most guidance on human-scale mathematics quietly assumes the answer is no. If it is yes, the profession becomes an exotic art with little funding, and the same would hold across science and engineering.
  • He remains optimistic, at least for many years, because LLMs still seem far from a useful sense of elegance for finding their way among possible theorems.

item.title: Digest — 21 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Gowers, Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — An experimental AI-math challenge: using tenth discriminant bounds to explore arguments ruling out Siegel zeroes

  • Tao launches an open, Polymath-style challenge: take each recent manuscript or write-up excluding Landau–Siegel zeroes (or proving a quasi-Riemann hypothesis) and use AI to extract an explicit upper bound on a hypothetical "tenth discriminant" in Gauss's class number one problem, without Heegner's method.
  • Background: Heilbronn–Linfoot's repulsion argument allowed at most one extra discriminant but was ineffective; Goldfeld (1976), then Oesterlé with the Gross–Zagier curve, made it effective. The new effective Siegel-zero arguments should each give such a bound, but making the constants explicit is tedious work well suited to AI.
  • Goals: compare the "strength" of competing write-ups, maybe a new Lean-formalizable (Mathlib-ready) solution of class number one, ideas for higher class numbers (solved up to 100 by Watkins), and possibly rescuing older failed attempts. Since the problem is solved, there's little risk of disrupting anyone's ongoing research.
  • Rules: any AI use allowed if disclosed, large outputs posted as GitHub links, outputs checked independently, credit given to earlier entries; quality over speed, and negative results (bad bounds) are welcome too. It follows his 19 October sketch of the Siegel-zero proof and his "Math 2.0" talk.
  • 👉 A concrete template for running AI-assisted collaborative research responsibly, worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts — Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?

  • An anonymous PhD student writes an open letter (part of a 19–23 October series for PhD applicants and students): after OpenAI's 6 October paper release, they have decided to leave academia after the doctorate.
  • The main argument: years of failing at hard technical problems are how a mathematician builds intuition and taste. A Math 2.0 where people curate and interpret AI output relies on experts trained the old way, and the letter says it never explains how it will train the next generation.
  • It also asks who such a profession will attract, and whether hiring and funding committees will reward slow independent work when peers turn out AI-assisted results.
  • Criticizes established mathematicians' enthusiasm, and Tao's Math 2.0 vision in particular, for ignoring what students want.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to PhD supervision: a clear statement of what some students fear.

Proofs and Prompts — A critique of the mathematical economy

  • Álvaro Gutiérrez (PhD student, Bristol) borrows Marx's labour theory of value to model mathematics as an economy: lemmas, proofs, examples, surveys and so on are "commodities".
  • He separates "true value" (the socially necessary labour time), use value (being reused in later work, which flows back to earlier papers), and realised value (referee reports, prizes, letters, jobs, grants).
  • LLMs cheapen all three: technical lemmas and counterexamples most of all, and attribution gets worse because models hide their sources. That fuels the fear that everyone must adopt AI to stay competitive, i.e. deskilling.
  • His twist: in mathematics there is no capitalist. Mathematicians themselves referee, hire and award prizes, so the community has more power than it thinks to decide what it values. He replies to David Bessis's "fall of the theorem economy".

Proofs and Prompts — Letter to a worried student

  • David A. Madore (Télécom Paris) publishes his email reply to a student wondering whether to leave mathematics, in English with the French original.
  • He shares the student's worries: AI companies treat open problems as trophies and a training ground, and say too little about their methods or their failed attempts for this to count as science.
  • He partly blames mathematicians themselves for prizing hard problems and races to results over understanding. He hopes research moves toward good questions, illuminating viewpoints and exposition.
  • His conclusion: understanding stays a human activity, and driving promising students away would be the worst harm AI could do to the field.
  • 👉 A voice from the French community, and a useful model for answering students who ask the same question.

item.title: Digest — 20 October 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new in the last 24 hours from Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Silicon Reckoner (Harris) or Tao's Mastodon.

Terence Tao — A sketch of the proof of non-existence of Siegel zeroes

  • Expository walk-through of the recent exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeroes, following Ben Green's streamlined version of a nine-page paper from OpenAI's math release (alongside two "quasi-Riemann hypothesis" papers giving zero-free strips with exponents 11/12 and 7/8). Banks (arXiv:2610.15483) and Kerr (arXiv:2610.21099) have produced their own digests.
  • Core estimate: primes with Legendre symbol (D/p) = −1 carry at most about half of the Mertens weight Σ log p / p; standard analytic arguments then recover the classical exp(−c√log x) error term without Siegel exceptions. Pescador and Barretto have sharper preprints.
  • Method ("adelic polynomial method"): take a lattice of integer polynomials, evaluate them with derivatives on a skewed grid of points m ± n√D, and study the integer M given by the squared covolume. Hadamard's inequality bounds |M| from above; Frobenius (the curve z₁^p = z₂ passes p-adically near every grid point when (D/p) = −1) forces large p-adic valuations; unique factorisation compares the two.
  • Non-degeneracy comes from a resultant argument exploiting the distinct second coordinates of the skew grid; Tao stresses the polynomial method is what breaks the parity barrier here, and asks readers for the history of the technique (Bombieri–Vaaler, Masser, Laurent).
  • Tao discloses that an AI chat helped him digest the preprints.

Proofs and Prompts — Recommendations on the use of AI for PhD students and supervisors

  • Guidelines from 37 symplectic geometers (incl. Auroux, Seidel, Smith, Keating, Cornea, Ginzburg), restricted to AI use for mathematical content, not editing or bibliography.
  • Students: engage with AI but verify every step yourself; keep a log of prompts and answers and disclose AI-derived content; AI is never a co-author; don't feed others' unpublished work to commercial models without consent. Expect more open-ended topics and higher standards of independence.
  • Supervisors: neither forbid nor impose AI; check whether a proposed problem could be dispatched quickly by a model; agree on documentation early; make sure core techniques and human contact are still learned; defenses should test real understanding of the new results.
  • Institutions: leave the choice of tools (commercial or local) to researchers, pay for them centrally, and set simple disclosure rules for theses.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: your field's community and PhD supervision; French signatories include Viterbo (Paris-Saclay), Oancea and Damian (Strasbourg), Gironella (Nantes), Mazzucchelli (Sorbonne).

Proofs and Prompts — Contribution, Credit, and Community

  • Tommaso Moraschini (philosophy, Barcelona) takes AI adoption as given and asks how credit should work afterwards.
  • Argues priority no longer signals insight and should stop counting as merit in itself; warns of a "Prompt or Perish" race, a flood of weak papers, and growing secrecy about partial results.
  • Considers AI disclosures unverifiable and liable to encourage concealment: comparable results should get equal credit whatever the tools, and abstaining from AI should not be rewarded.
  • Proposals: hiring that weighs exposition and vision (seminars, interviews, franker letters), and larger collaborative groups on exploratory programmes to defuse competition.
